The Lombards were a Germanic people who invaded and settled northern Italy in 568 under Alboin, conquering the Po Valley and much of the peninsula after the chaos of the Gothic Wars had weakened Byzantine control. They established a decentralized kingdom ruled by dukes in different regions, creating the first medieval Italian political fragmentation that would persist for centuries. Gradually, the Lombards adopted Roman law and Catholic Christianity, blending Germanic and Roman institutions into a hybrid kingdom that served as a bridge to medieval Europe. They produced remarkable legal documents, including the Edict of Rothari, a written law code showing sophisticated administration and legal thought. Unlike the Ostrogoths or Visigoths, the Lombards did not vanish entirely when their kingdom fell. Charlemagne conquered their kingdom in 774, ending Lombard independence and bringing Italy under Frankish authority, yet they were absorbed into the Frankish sphere rather than destroyed, and their cultural influence persisted in northern Italian society. The Lombards also controlled key Alpine passes and trade routes, making them economically important to early medieval Europe. Their name would survive in the northern Italian region of Lombardy, and their legal traditions influenced the medieval systems that followed.
